back: [[kw:Statistics]] is the [[imp:science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data]] to make decisions.
It turns raw numbers into [[imp:informed decisions]].
[[kw:Data]] are [[imp:information from observations, counts, measurements, or responses]].
They can be numbers (quantitative) or labels (qualitative).
A [[kw:population]] is the [[imp:complete collection]] of all items of interest.
Think “whole group” – for example, all adults in the U.S.
A [[kw:sample]] is a [[imp:subset]] of a population.
We use samples because measuring an entire population is usually [[imp:impractical]].
A [[kw:census]] collects data from [[imp:every member]] of a population.
It's often too expensive or time‑consuming for large groups.
A [[kw:parameter]] is a [[imp:numerical description of a population]].
It's fixed (usually unknown). Memory tip: [[imp:P]]arameter ↔ [[imp:P]]opulation.
A [[kw:statistic]] is a [[imp:numerical description of a sample]].
It varies from sample to sample. Memory tip: [[imp:S]]tatistic ↔ [[imp:S]]ample.

cards.front: Which varies from sample to sample — [[kw:parameter]] or [[kw:statistic]]?
back: A [[kw:statistic]] varies; a [[kw:parameter]] stays [[imp:constant]] (though unknown).
Different samples give different statistics.

cards.front: How are a [[kw:statistic]] and a [[kw:parameter]] connected?
back: We use a sample [[kw:statistic]] to [[imp:estimate]] the unknown population [[kw:parameter]].
The statistic is our best guess for the parameter.
[[kw:Descriptive statistics]] [[imp:organizes, summarizes, and displays]] data.
Tools: charts, averages, percentages. It stays within the sample.
[[kw:Inferential statistics]] [[imp:uses a sample to draw conclusions]] about a population.
It relies on [[imp:probability]] to make inferences.

cards.front: 70% of unmarried men lived to 65 vs. 90% of married men. Which part is descriptive?
back: The [[kw:percentages]] (70% and 90%) are [[kw:descriptive]].
A possible [[kw:inferential]] conclusion: [[imp:Marriage is associated with longer life.]]
[[imp:Representative]] of the population.
If a sample is [[imp:biased]], conclusions are unreliable.
cards.front: What must a sample be for valid conclusions?
What is the difference between [[kw:qualitative data]] and [[kw:quantitative data]]?
back: [[kw:Qualitative data]]: [[imp:labels, attributes, or nonnumerical entries]] (e.g., car models, eye colors).
[[kw:Quantitative data]]: [[imp:numerical measurements or counts]] (e.g., prices, heights, home runs).
Key test: can you do meaningful arithmetic on the numbers?
Types of TV shows (comedy, drama, sports).
Jersey numbers (used as labels, not measurements).
Political party (Democrat, Republican, Independent).
[[imp:Even if numbers appear, they may be qualitative if they act as labels.]]
Weights of infants at a hospital.
Number of home runs hit by a team.
Lengths of songs on an MP3 player.
[[imp:These are numbers you can add, average, or compare in meaningful ways.]]
[[imp:Categorization only.]] No order, no meaningful differences.
Examples: types of shows, network call letters, eye colors.
Even if numbers are used (e.g., jersey numbers), they are nominal when they only label.
Data can be [[imp:arranged in order or ranked]], but differences are not meaningful.
Examples: TV show rankings (#1, #2, #3...), MPAA ratings (G, PG, PG‑13...), class rank.
The gap between ranks may not be equal.
Order and [[imp:meaningful differences]] are allowed.
[[imp:No true zero]] — zero is just a position on a scale.
Ratios don't make sense (e.g., 40°F is not “twice as hot” as 20°F).
Examples: temperature in °F or °C, calendar years.
Has all properties of interval, plus a [[imp:true zero]] that means “none.”
Ratios are meaningful: $20 is twice $10.
Examples: prices, heights, weights, rainfall amounts, home run totals.

cards.front: How do you test whether data are interval or ratio?
back: Ask: “Does zero mean [[imp:complete absence]] of what I'm measuring?”
If yes → [[kw:ratio]]. If zero is just a point on a scale → [[kw:interval]].
Example: 0°F doesn't mean no heat (interval); $0 means no money (ratio).

cards.front: What are the four levels of measurement in order from lowest to highest?
back: [[kw:Nominal]] — categories only.
[[kw:Ordinal]] — categories + order.
[[kw:Interval]] — categories + order + meaningful differences, no true zero.
[[kw:Ratio]] — categories + order + differences + true zero and ratios.
[[imp:Always assign the highest level that applies.]]

cards.front: Are jersey numbers (e.g., 23, 45) qualitative or quantitative? What level?
back: [[kw:Qualitative]] — they are [[imp:labels]], not measurements.
Adding them gives meaningless results.
Level: [[kw:nominal]].
[[kw:Quantitative]] (ranks are numbers) or [[kw:qualitative]]? They represent order.
They can be ordered, but differences between ranks aren't meaningful as viewer counts.
Level: [[kw:ordinal]].
cards.front: Classify TV show rankings (#1 American Idol, #2 Dancing with the Stars).

back: [[kw:Quantitative]] — a measurement.
Can be ordered, differences are meaningful.
But 0°F is not absolute zero heat.
Level: [[kw:interval]].
cards.front: Classify body temperature (in °F) of an athlete.
Classify the weight of an athlete.
back: [[kw:Quantitative]].
Order, meaningful differences, a true zero (0 lbs means no weight).
Can say one athlete weighs twice as much as another.
Level: [[kw:ratio]].

cards.front: What is the key takeaway for classifying data by type and level?
back: First decide type: [[kw:qualitative]] (labels) or [[kw:quantitative]] (numbers for math).
Then run the level checklist: categories? order? differences? true zero? ratios?
[[imp:Context matters — a number could be nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio depending on what it represents.]]

cards.front: Identify [[kw:population]] and [[kw:sample]]: 1,500 U.S. adults surveyed about global warming.
back: [[kw:Population]]: [[imp:all U.S. adults]].
[[kw:Sample]]: [[imp:the 1,500 surveyed]].
Data: 855 yes, 645 no.

cards.front: All 2,182 admitted students at a university have an average SAT of 1442. Is 1442 a [[kw:parameter]] or a [[kw:statistic]]?
back: [[kw:Parameter]] — it describes the [[imp:entire population of admitted students]].
No sampling occurred; the whole group was measured.
That the sample accurately reflects the [[imp:characteristics of the population]].
Without it, any inference about the population is unreliable.
